summary.text:
Liverpool City Region Combined Authority 2025/26 Treasury Management Outturn Report (Appendix 5 to the Combined Authority Financial Outturn 2025/26 and 2026/27 Budget Revisions), taken to the CA on 17 July 2026 and approved. Adviser not named in this appendix. Contact Officers on the covering report: Claire Hall, Director of Finance, and Veronica Wilson, Strategic Finance Manager.

Position at 31 March 2026. External debt £261.334m — PWLB £111.826m at 5.40% weighted (avg life 13.74yr) and EIB £149.508m at 1.51% weighted (avg life 24.71yr). Investments £325.835m treasury, £14.958m non-treasury. Net debt (£64.501m) — a net-investor position at year end. CFR £656.921m; ROU lease liability £38.992m; internal borrowing £356.595m (54% of CFR), closing the balance-sheet identity to the pound against Table Three's '(Under)/over funding of CFR' line.

Loan-book reconciliation TIES on principal. Our price_book returns 25 PWLB loans totalling £111,825,740 at 5.4831% weighted against their Table Five figure of £111,826k at 5.40% — principal delta £260 (0.0002%); rate delta +8bp, most likely presentation rounding since the paper prints to one decimal. Balance-sheet identity closes exactly. The EIB tranche is outside our data (we hold PWLB only), which we should be explicit about.

Three hooks the email is built on. First, the reconciliation opener — one sentence, tied to Table Five, which settles that the reading was real before anything else lands. Second, the shape of the book: EIB at £149.5m is 57% of external debt by principal and runs at 1.51%, giving a blended cost across PWLB + EIB of c3.17% — an unusual profile among the councils we have read, most of whom rely on PWLB alone. Third, the pivot the paper itself signals for 2026/27 — Appendix A shows the Liability Benchmark flipping from (£12.23m) in 2025/26 outturn to +£82.16m in 2026/27, an £94m swing, and the Financing Cost to Net Revenue Stream ratio nearly doubling from 7.59% to 13.05% in the same step. §3.33–3.34 explains: the Rolling Stock programme was expected to trigger EIB and PWLB drawings in 2025/26 but was successfully deferred thanks to favourable cashflow. That deferral has now compressed into the 2026/27 numbers, alongside a £407m capital programme year (up from £288m). PWLB reference rates at 31 March 2026 are printed at §3.30 (1y 5.04%, 5y 5.28%, 10y 5.72%, 25y 6.29%, 50y 6.08%); between then and 14 August the long end has risen 6-19bp with Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75%.

What is not raised: our indicative break-cost figures (paper is explicit at §3.34 that no rescheduling was undertaken; not a productive hook); the 8bp rate delta on the reconciliation (rounding, do not raise as a discrepancy); the £1.07m residual between the balance-sheet-derived internal borrowing and Appendix A's 'Gross Debt and CFR' £357.66m (rounding at £m scale); the investment income outperformance detail (paper has already surfaced it — §3.38 attributes to laddering and favourable cash). The Contact Officer named on the covering report is Claire Hall (Director of Finance); she is not explicitly named as S151 in this paper. The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts identifies the S151 as the Executive Director – Resources, unnamed on this outturn's front sheets. Address to Claire Hall using her printed title only.

Meeting on 17 July 2026 is past. Next natural treasury item is the mid-year 2026/27 report to the CA in December 2026 (per §2.2 pattern; no firm date printed). Send_by targets late November 2026.

officer.body:
Dear Claire,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority and combined authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every authority's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data and the training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on your 2025/26 Treasury Management Outturn (Appendix 5), taken to the Combined Authority on 17 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. It's a clearly laid out paper and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

As a cross-check that our numbers tie to yours: Table Five gives PWLB debt of £111,826k at 5.40% weighted. Our file carries 25 PWLB loans against your name (HALTON KNOWSLEY LIVERPOOL ETC CA in the DMO series) totalling £111,825,740 as at 31 March, so we tie to £260 on principal — the weighted rate reads 5.48% on our side against your 5.40%, likely just rounding to one decimal. Each of the 25 loans is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

What sits alongside is what makes the position distinctive. The £149.5m EIB tranche runs at 1.51% weighted with average life 24.71 years — a very different animal to the PWLB book. Blended, external debt costs about 3.17% overall, well below where a PWLB-only book of similar size would sit. Of the roughly 80 councils and combined authorities we've read this year, that EIB share is one of the largest we hold sight of. We don't carry EIB loans in our data, so we can't reconcile that line the way we can the PWLB one — worth flagging honestly.

The other thing worth flagging is the pivot the paper prints for 2026/27. Appendix A puts the Liability Benchmark at (£12.23m) for 2025/26 — small net-investor — flipping to +£82.16m for 2026/27 before easing to £43.63m and £25.86m. That's a £94m swing in one year. In the same column, Financing Costs as a Proportion of Net Revenue Stream go from 7.59% to 13.05% — nearly a doubling. Paragraphs 3.33 and 3.34 explain: the Rolling Stock programme was expected to trigger EIB and PWLB drawings in 2025/26 but favourable cashflow deferred them, and the 2026/27 capital plan sits at £407m against £288m this year.

Which is why the rate curve you'd face when the drawings do happen is worth watching. Paragraph 3.30 prints the PWLB Certainty rates at 31 March as 5.04%, 5.28%, 5.72%, 6.29% and 6.08% at 1, 5, 10, 25 and 50 years. On the 14 August PM fixing those are 5.34% at 5 years, 5.83% at 10 and 6.27% at 50 — 6 to 19 basis points higher, with Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75%. The direction of travel between March and August has been mildly against the strategy assumption at §3.23 that medium-to-long borrowing costs would ease through 2026 and 2027. Daily fixings at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

On training, "Liability Benchmark: using it in practice" sits directly on the (£12m) → +£82m pivot; "Strategic PWLB borrowing" picks up the choice of maturity and profile when the deferred drawings happen; "MRP — policy options and revenue impact" covers what your £17.6m annual charge is doing to the CFR path. All 115 courses are free to authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team. One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put the LB in front of every S151: our interactive LB pathway lets you stress the reserves and cashflow paths directly — pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
